style_when: the article describes one decisive moment or place — a yard at dawn, a control room, a shutdown line, a handover — that a film still could hold
prompt: 35mm anamorphic wide photograph, shallow depth of field, fine film grain. A lone unbranded last-mile delivery truck with engine off and dark instrument cluster, parked at a loading bay, off-centre right in an asymmetric low-angle frame. A single amber overhead yard light from the left carves long shadows across a wet concrete apron; behind it a galvanised steel dock door, graphite and bone white with a safety-yellow bollard at the frame edge. No driver, no people, no logos, no text. Deep blue-hour darkness outside, chiaroscuro.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, watermarks, illegible signage
rationale: Cinematic still captures the decisive operational gap: a truck at rest between logged events, the environment carrying the weight of invisible stops rather than a sterile abstraction. The wide anamorphic frame and single practical light give editorial tension without falling into datacenter or form clichés.
subject: an unbranded last-mile delivery truck with engine off and dark instrument cluster, parked at a loading bay
core_thesis: A last-mile carbon number is a fuel total multiplied by a published factor, but the federal ELD file resolves engine time to six-minute slices, whole miles, and positions only at logged events, so the yearly total can be sound while every stop-level split is a model.
core_conflict: Sound annual fuel total vs coarse six-minute event logging that erases stop-level delivery resolution.
composition: asymmetric low-angle 16:9 framing, truck off-centre right with deep loading-bay perspective receding left
alt_text: Unbranded last-mile delivery truck with engine off, parked alone in a loading bay under a single amber light, long shadows across concrete.
caption: The federal log behind a carrier's carbon number is built for hours, not per-stop fuel.
title: Carbon Data Stops At 6 Minutes

review.depicts: A white cab-over box truck with no company markings parked on wet asphalt in front of a corrugated metal warehouse wall at night, with two roll-up loading doors and a wall-mounted lamp illuminating the bay behind it.
review.reason: The frame shows the article's own protagonist — an unbranded last-mile delivery truck parked at a loading bay — which is the vehicle whose six-minute federal activity record the carbon number is built from, though the image itself carries no hint of the data or carbon mechanism.
